Female Argentine shortfin squid (Illex argentinus) reach a maximum dorsal mantle length of 34.4 centimeters [Li = 34.4 centimeters] at the time of natural death, a size that reflects the substantial somatic growth achieved during their approximately one-year life cycle. Males are slightly smaller at senescence, attaining a terminal mantle length of 34.0 centimeters [Li = 34.0 centimeters]. Sexual maturation in this species is size-dependent rather than strictly age-dependent, with females entering puberty upon reaching a mantle length of 26.0 centimeters [Lp = 26.0 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to a broad range of 195 to 330 millimeters reported across different oceanographic sectors of the Southwest Atlantic. Males initiate gonadal development at a notably smaller body size, with puberty observed at a mantle length of 20.0 centimeters [Lp = 20.0 centimeters], corresponding to a documented range of 142 to 250 millimeters. This sexual dimorphism in maturation size is consistent with the pattern observed in many ommastrephid squids, wherein females invest more heavily in somatic growth before allocating resources to reproductive tissues.

The initial body mass at the onset of exogenous feeding is remarkably low, as newly hatched paralarvae possess a wet weight of just 0.001 grams [Wwb = 0.001 grams], a value derived from the estimated volume of the cylindrical larval body form measuring approximately 2 millimeters in length and 0.8 millimeters in width. This minute birth mass reflects the minimal yolk reserves available to the embryo at the time of hatching, necessitating an immediate transition to planktivorous feeding in the upper water column. Pelagic paralarvae of Illex argentinus are thus among the smallest cephalopod hatchlings documented, with a body plan that prioritizes rapid surface-area-driven nutrient absorption and early foraging capability. The transition from endogenous to exogenous feeding occurs within the first few days post-hatching, coinciding with the complete resorption of the internal yolk sac, at which point the digestive tract becomes fully functional for processing microzooplankton.

At the termination of their life cycle, reproductively spent females attain a total wet body mass of 1500.0 grams [Wwi = 1500.0 grams], an estimate based on species-specific length-weight relationships scaled from morphometric data available for the closely related jumbo squid Dosidicus gigas. This substantial terminal mass represents the culmination of a rapid growth trajectory that spans just under one year under typical thermal conditions. The cumulative reproductive output at the moment of senescence in females maintained at a stable water temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C] reaches approximately 750,000 oocytes , representing a massive single investment in gamete production typical of semelparous ommastrephids. This high fecundity compensates for the extremely high rates of early-life mortality characteristic of pelagic spawning strategies, where both eggs and paralarvae face intense predation pressure from a wide array of zooplanktonic and nektonic consumers.

The maximum lifespan documented for female Argentine shortfin squid under controlled laboratory conditions at a constant temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C] is 365.0 days [am = 365.0 days], a duration that aligns closely with field-based estimates from statolith increment analysis conducted on wild-caught specimens from the Patagonian shelf. This annual life cycle, which encompasses a single synchronized spawning event followed by rapid senescence and mortality, classifies Illex argentinus as a true annual species. The consistency between laboratory longevity data and field-derived age estimates suggests that environmental temperature exerts a strong influence on the metabolic clock governing somatic and reproductive development. Males typically exhibit slightly shorter lifespans than females, although the difference is marginal and falls within the interannual variability observed across different cohorts.

Energy allocation during the reproductive phase is heavily weighted toward a single explosive spawning event, with females producing a cumulative fecundity at death of 750,000 eggs , delivered in multiple successive batches over a brief period of days to weeks, all while the individual experiences progressive physiological deterioration at a temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C]. The terminal body mass of females reaches approximately 1500 grams [Wwi = approximately 1500 grams] at the conclusion of this reproductive effort, a mass that represents the maximum achievable under the species' life-history constraints. Comparative data from related ommastrephids suggest that the relatively large terminal body size of Illex argentinus, coupled with its high fecundity, is an adaptation to the highly productive but temporally variable waters of the Patagonian shelf-break front, where pulsed food availability supports rapid growth and sustained oocyte production before the onset of spawning-associated mortality.
